title: Chapter 113 — The Forge
paragraphs: With matted beard and swathed in a bristling shark-skin apron, about midday Perth was standing between his forge and anvil, the latter placed upon an ironwood log, with one hand holding a pike-head in the coals and with the other at his forge's bellows, when Captain Ahab came along, carrying in his hands a small rustic bag of studded leather.
"Are these your Mother Carey's chickens, Perth? They are always flying in your wake; birds of good omen, too, but not to all — look here, they burn; but you — you live among them without a scorch."
"Because I am scorched all over, Captain Ahab," answered Perth, resting for a moment on his hammer; "I am past scorching; not easily can you scorch a scar."

"Well, well; no more. Your shrunken voice sounds too calmly, sanely woeful to me. In no Paradise myself, I am impatient of all misery in others that is not mad. You should go mad, blacksmith; say, why don't you go mad? How can you endure without being mad? Do the heavens yet hate you, that you cannot go mad? What are you working at?"
"Welding an old pike-head, sir; there were seams and dents in it."
"And can you make it all smooth again, blacksmith, after such hard usage as it had?"
"I think so, sir."
"And I suppose you can smooth almost any seams and dents; never mind how hard the metal, blacksmith?"
"Aye, sir, I think I can; all seams and dents but one."

"Look here, then," cried Ahab, passionately advancing, and leaning with both hands on Perth's shoulders; "look here — here — can you smooth out a seam like this, blacksmith?" sweeping one hand across his furrowed brow; "if you could, blacksmith, glad enough would I lay my head upon your anvil, and feel your heaviest hammer between my eyes. Answer! Can you smooth this seam?"
"Oh! That is the one, sir! Did I not say all seams and dents but one?"

"Aye, blacksmith, it is the one; aye, man, it is unsmoothable; for though you only see it here in my flesh, it has worked down into the bone of my skull — that is all wrinkles! But away with child's play; no more hooks and pikes today. Look here!" jingling the leather bag as if it were full of gold coins; "I, too, want a harpoon made; one that a thousand devils could not part. Something that will stick in a whale like his own fin-bone. There's the stuff," flinging the pouch upon the anvil. "Look, blacksmith, these are the gathered nail-stubs of the steel shoes of racing horses."
"Horseshoe stubs, sir? Why, Captain Ahab, you have here, then, the best and stubbornest stuff we blacksmiths ever work."

"I know it, old man; these stubs will weld together like glue from the melted bones of murderers. Quick! Forge me the harpoon. And forge me first twelve rods for its shank; then wind and twist and hammer these twelve together like the yarns and strands of a tow-line. Quick! I'll blow the fire."

When at last the twelve rods were made, Ahab tried them, one by one, by spiraling them with his own hand round a long, heavy iron bolt. "A flaw!" rejecting the last one. "Work that over again, Perth."

This done, Perth was about to begin welding the twelve into one, when Ahab stayed his hand and said he would weld his own iron. As, then, with regular, gasping heaves, he hammered on the anvil, Perth passing him the glowing rods one after another, and the hard-pressed forge shooting up its intense straight flame, the Parsee passed silently, and bowing over his head toward the fire, seemed invoking some curse or some blessing upon the toil. But, as Ahab looked up, he slid aside.

"What's that bunch of fireflies dodging about there for?" muttered Stubb, looking on from the forecastle. "That Parsee smells fire like a fuse; and smells of it himself, like a hot musket's powder-pan."
At last the shank, in one complete rod, received its final heat; and as Perth, to temper it, plunged it all hissing into the cask of water near by, the scalding steam shot up into Ahab's bent face.
"Would you brand me, Perth?" wincing for a moment with the pain; "have I been but forging my own branding-iron, then?"
"Pray God, not that; yet I fear something, Captain Ahab. Is not this harpoon for the White Whale?"
"For the white fiend! But now for the barbs; you must make them yourself, man. Here are my razors — the best of steel; here, and make the barbs sharp as the needle-sleet of the Icy Sea."
For a moment, the old blacksmith eyed the razors as though he would rather not use them.
"Take them, man, I have no need for them; for I now neither shave, sup, nor pray till — but here — to work!"

Fashioned at last into an arrow-shape and welded by Perth to the shank, the steel soon pointed the end of the iron; and as the blacksmith was about to give the barbs their final heat, prior to tempering them, he cried to Ahab to place the water-cask near.

"No, no — no water for that; I want it of the true death-temper. Ahoy, there! Tashtego, Queequeg, Daggoo! What say you, pagans! Will you give me as much blood as will cover this barb?" holding it high up. A cluster of dark nods replied: Yes. Three punctures were made in the heathen flesh, and the White Whale's barbs were then tempered.
"Ego non baptizo te in nomine patris, sed in nomine diaboli!" deliriously howled Ahab, as the malignant iron scorchingly devoured the baptismal blood.

Now, mustering the spare poles from below and selecting one of hickory, with the bark still on it, Ahab fitted the end to the socket of the iron. A coil of new tow-line was then unwound, and some fathoms of it taken to the windlass and stretched to a great tension. Pressing his foot upon it, till the rope hummed like a harp-string, then eagerly bending over it and seeing no strandings, Ahab exclaimed: "Good! and now for the seizings."

At one end the rope was unstranded, and the separate spread yarns were all braided and woven round the socket of the harpoon; the pole was then driven hard up into the socket; from the lower end the rope was traced halfway along the pole's length, and firmly secured so, with intertwistings of twine; and then, as the line stretched beyond that, its outer extremity was looped back upon itself into the body of the line, forming a spring. The completed weapon was now presented to Ahab.
